edition.name: Migne, Patrologia Latina (PL 1, Paris 1844), De patientia, via Latin Wikisource transcription
edition.witness_note: Single locked witness in repo; second witness not yet locked.

source_text: Ipsa adeo est, quae fidem, et subsequitur, et antecedit. Denique Abraham Deo credidit, et justitiae deputatus ab illo est: sed fidem ejus patientia probavit, cum filium immolare jussus est, ad fidei non tentationem dixerim, sed typicam contestationem. Caeterum Deus, quem justitiae deputasset, sciebat. Tam grave praeceptum, quod nec Domino perfici placebat, patienter et audivit, et si Deus voluisset, implesset. Merito ergo benedictus, quia et fidelis; merito fidelis, quia et patiens. Ita fides patientia illuminata, cum in nationes seminaretur per semen Abrahae, quod est Christus, et gratiam legi superduceret, ampliandae adimplendaeque legi adjutricem suam patientiam praefecit, quod ea sola ad justitiae doctrinam retro defuisset. Nam olim et oculum pro oculo, et dentem pro dente repetebant, et malum malo foenerabant: nondum enim patientia in terris, quia nec fides: scilicet interim impatientia occasionibus legis fruebatur. Facile erat, absente domino patientiae et magistro. Qui postquam supervenit, et gratiam fidei patientia composuit, jam nec verbo quidem lacessere, nec Fatue quidem dicere sine judicii periculo licet. Prohibita ira, restricti animi, compressa petulantia manus, exemptum linguae venenum, plus lex quam amisit invenit, dicente Christo: Diligite inimicos vestros, et maledicentibus benedicite: et orate pro persecutoribus vestris, ut filii sitis Patris vestri coelestis. Vides quem nobis patrem patientia acquirat? Hoc principali praecepto universa patientiae disciplina succincta est, quando ne digne quidem malefacere concessum est.
pass_a_gloss: It itself is, which faith, and follows, and precedes. Finally Abraham believed God, and was reckoned to justice by Him: but patience proved his faith, when he was ordered to slay his son, to the testing of faith, I say not, but a symbolic proof. Moreover God, who had reckoned him to justice, knew. So grave a command, which not even the Lord was pleased to fulfill, he heard patiently, and would have fulfilled, if God had willed. Deservedly therefore blessed, because also faithful; deservedly faithful, because also patient. Thus faith illuminated by patience, when it was being sown among the nations through the seed of Abraham, which is Christ, and was bringing grace over the law, patience was set as its helper for amplifying and fulfilling the law, because alone it had previously been lacking for the doctrine of justice. For once they used to demand an eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth, and lend evil for evil: for patience was not yet on earth, because neither was faith: evidently meanwhile impatience was enjoying the occasions of the law. It was easy, with the lord of patience and its teacher absent. Who after He arrived, and composed patience with the grace of faith, now not even with a word is it allowed to provoke, nor even to say 'Fool' without danger of judgment. Anger is prohibited, spirits are restrained, the petulance of hands is compressed, the venom of the tongue is removed, the law finds more than it lost, with Christ saying: Love your enemies, and bless those who curse you: and pray for your persecutors, so that you may be sons of your heavenly Father. You see what father patience acquires for us? By this principal command the whole discipline of patience is summarized, when not even to do evil in return is allowed.

choices.why: to convey the idea of a test or proof that is symbolic or representative
to translate the Latin word 'Fatue' as 'Fool', which is a strong insult
to translate the Latin phrase as a direct quote from Christ

bible_refs.note: Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you

pass_b_english: It is patience itself that both follows faith and precedes it. Take Abraham: he believed God, and God reckoned it to him as justice; yet patience proved his faith when he was ordered to sacrifice his son—not, I should say, as a test of faith, but as a symbolic witness. God, who had reckoned him just, knew the heart of the matter. Abraham heard so grave a command—one that not even the Lord was willing to carry out—patiently, and he would have fulfilled it had God so willed. Deservedly, then, is he called blessed, because he was faithful; deservedly faithful, because he was patient. Thus faith, illuminated by patience, when it was being sown among the nations through the seed of Abraham, which is Christ, and was bringing grace to supersede the law, appointed patience as its helper for amplifying and fulfilling the law, because patience alone had previously been lacking for the doctrine of justice. In former times they used to demand an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth, and to return evil for evil, because patience was not yet on earth—nor was faith—and so impatience enjoyed the occasions the law provided. It was easy enough when the lord and teacher of patience was absent. But after he arrived and joined patience to the grace of faith, it is no longer permitted even to provoke with a word, nor even to say 'Fool' without danger of judgment. Anger is prohibited, spirits are restrained, the petulance of hands is curbed, the venom of the tongue is removed, and the law finds more than it lost, Christ saying: 'Love your enemies, and bless those who curse you, and pray for your persecutors, so that you may be sons of your heavenly Father' (Matthew 5:44; Luke 6:27-28). You see what Father patience acquires for us? By this principal command the whole discipline of patience is summed up, when not even to return evil is allowed.
